title: A common germline 3' UTR variant controls DDIT4 translation efficiency and stress responses in cancer cells.
abstract: Systematic strategies for identifying and classifying variants that directly modulate ribosome engagement are lacking. Here, we develop and extensively validate a pipeline to identify translation-associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (tranSNPs) by integrating analysis of total and polysome-associated mRNAs. Common variants showing allele-specific enrichment in polysomes, without corresponding changes in mRNA levels, were uncovered. We focused on rs1053639, a frequent germline SNP located in the 3' UTR of DNA damage-inducible transcript 4 (DDIT4), a key negative regulator of mTORC1. Using edited cell models, we showed that this variant controls DDIT4 protein output. Mechanistically, the two rs1053639 alleles differ in their interaction with the RNA-binding protein RBMX, leading to altered mRNA subcellular localization and translation. Functionally, allele-specific regulation of DDIT4 translation impacts stress-dependent mTORC1 repression and autophagy, resulting in divergent competitive fitness in co-culture or xenograft assays and response to therapeutic perturbations. Analysis of cancer patient datasets revealed an association between rs1053639 genotype and clinical outcome in colorectal cancer.

title: Endothelial Matrin-3 Limits Cellular Senescence and Lipid Dysregulation to Protect Against Murine Atherosclerosis.
abstract: Matrin-3 is a DNA- and RNA-binding protein implicated in cardiovascular development. However, the role of endothelial Matrin-3 in atherosclerosis has not been previously studied. Here, we found that Matrin-3 silencing induces endothelial senescence, characterized by reduced cell proliferation, increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity, and impaired mitochondrial function in vitro. Quantitative proteomics and bulk RNA-sequencing identified hundreds of differentially expressed genes and proteins in human endothelial cells. Bioinformatic analyses revealed enrichment of pathways related to DNA replication, p53 signaling, cell-cycle regulation, and cellular senescence. To examine the role of endothelial Matrin-3 in atherosclerosis, we generated Matrin-3 floxed mice on a low-density lipoprotein receptor-knockout background and crossed them with mice carrying an endothelial cell-specific, tamoxifen-inducible Cre driver. In a mouse model of atherosclerosis, endothelial cell-specific Matrin-3 deficiency increased atherosclerotic lesion area by 1.41-fold and was associated with increased plasma low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides, increased hepatic cholesterol and triglycerides, and substantial transcriptional alterations in the aortic intima. Endothelial Matrin-3 deficiency also induced hepatic steatosis, fibrosis, inflammation, and endothelial senescence. Single-nucleus RNA-sequencing of the liver further revealed transcriptional reprogramming of hepatocytes, including alterations in pathways related to lipid metabolism, inflammation, and constitutive androstane receptor signaling, consistent with a functional link between endothelial Matrin-3 deficiency and hepatocyte transcriptional responses. Finally, Matrin-3 expression was reduced in mouse and human atherosclerotic plaques. Together, these findings identify endothelial Matrin-3 as an important regulator of endothelial senescence and lipid homeostasis and demonstrate that endothelial Matrin-3 deficiency is associated with both local vascular alterations and systemic metabolic dysfunction in atherosclerosis.

title: ALYREF regulates glycolysis and promotes the progression of endometrial cancer through m5C modification of PKM2 mRNA.
abstract: Endometrial cancer (EC) is one of the most common gynecologic malignancies, and effective treatment options for advanced or recurrent cases remain limited. Here, we investigated the biological function and molecular mechanism of the RNA-binding protein ALYREF in EC. Bioinformatics analysis of public datasets revealed that ALYREF is significantly upregulated in EC tissues, and high ALYREF expression is associated with poor overall survival in the Kaplan-Meier Plotter cohort. Clinical validation using paired EC tissues confirmed ALYREF upregulation at protein level, and high ALYREF expression was associated with aggressive clinicopathological features. Functional assays revealed that ALYREF promotes EC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion in vitro and enhances tumor growth and metastasis in vivo. Mechanistically, ALYREF increases the stability of PKM2 mRNA, which we demonstrate to be m5C-modified in EC, leading to elevated PKM2 protein expression, enhanced glycolytic metabolism and tumor progression. Rescue experiments confirmed that PKM2 is an important downstream effector of ALYREF-mediated oncogenic activity. Collectively, this study identifies the ALYREF-PKM2 axis as an important regulator linking RNA methylation and glucose metabolism in EC, suggesting that this axis may be a potential therapeutic target for EC.

title: CasNano: An ultracompact CRISPR-Cas12f with a GC-rich PAM for epigenome editing with therapeutic potential.
abstract: Clinical use of CRISPR-Cas proteins for genome engineering is constrained by their large size, limiting in vivo delivery. To address this, we engineered an ultracompact and versatile platform from a minimally active, 400-amino acid Cas12f protein from Blautia lenta. A multi-stage strategy of structure-guided protein mutagenesis and systematic single guide RNA (sgRNA) optimization transformed BlCas12f into a "CasNano" as a potent genome targeting tool for mammalian cells. When a catalytically dead CasNano (dCasNano) is fused to a VPR domain, it activates endogenous genes with an efficiency and specificity comparable or superior to the benchmark SpCas9 system for the guide RNAs (gRNAs) and loci tested under equal-mass plasmid transfection; as editor expression was not quantified and stoichiometric differences would, in any case, preclude equivalent normalization, these comparisons describe functional output rather than intrinsic activity. We established the platform's versatility for bidirectional epigenetic editing by fusing dCasNano to a DNA methyltransferase (DNMT3A) for gene silencing or a dioxygenase (TET1) for gene activation. TET1-mediated reactivation persisted for 5 months in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), whereas DNMT3A-deposited methylation was not retained at 2 weeks in a dividing reporter line. CasNano's small size and distinct CCN PAM sequence highlight its potential for future therapeutic applications constrained by viral delivery cargo capacity.

title: Virus-encoded circular RNAs in human cancer: mechanisms and clinical implications.
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed RNA molecules generated mainly through back-splicing. Their resistance to exonuclease-mediated degradation, cell-type specificity, and regulatory versatility make them important participants in both host and viral biology. Since the initial demonstration that circular DNA tumor viruses produce abundant circRNAs, an expanding repertoire of virus-encoded circular RNAs (viro-circRNAs) has been identified in Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and related animal tumor viruses. Accumulating evidence indicates that viro-circRNAs are not passive transcriptional by-products; rather, they function as miRNA sponges, RNA-binding protein scaffolds, modulators of RNA stability and transcription, epigenetic or epitranscriptomic regulators, and in selected cases, templates for viral peptide or oncoprotein translation. Recent studies have refined this field by revealing noncanonical herpesvirus-driven circRNA biogenesis, EBV circRPMS1-mediated METTL3 activation and p53 interaction, hypoxia-induced EBV circLMP2A-driven angiogenesis, HPV16 circE7-mediated immune evasion through promoter histone modification, HBV-derived circRNA signaling in hepatocellular carcinoma, and HCV-derived circRNAs that support viral RNA amplification. In this review, we synthesize current evidence using a mechanistic and clinically oriented framework: first defining viro-circRNA biogenesis and validation, then summarizing virus- and cancer-specific expression patterns, followed by a detailed analysis of direct tumor-cell mechanisms, tumor microenvironment remodeling, biomarker potential, therapeutic opportunities, and unresolved challenges. This framework is intended to move the discussion beyond descriptive cataloguing and toward testable hypotheses for translational viro-circRNA research.

title: Identification of a novel, expressed, alternatively spliced FCER1G protein that inhibits receptor function.
abstract: The ITAM-containing FcRγ chain, encoded by FCER1G, non-covalently couples with the immunoglobulin-binding receptors, -- FcγRI (CD64), FcγRIIIa (CD16), FcϵRI and FcαRI (CD89), -- to initiate intracellular signals and mediate phagocytosis, cytokine production and other functions. While functionally impactful variants have been identified in the ligand-binding alpha-chains of receptors associated with FcRγ, variants in the signal-generating FcRγ have not been explored. Signal modulation through structural FcRγ variants would have implications for FcRγ-associated receptors and their role in immune-mediated diseases. We carried out in silico analyses of whole genome DNA sequence databases based on short-read sequencing of ~76, 000 genomes, long-read sequencing of 1132 genomes, whole exome sequences of ~800, 000 participants and RNA transcript databases. We used the hg38 reference genome to identify genomic DNA and cDNA structural variants and Sanger sequencing of cDNAs derived from FcRγ mRNAs isolated from local participants to confirm ESTs in circulating immune cells. To detect a putative novel alternatively spliced translated protein (AS-FcRγ), we developed isoform-specific monoclonal antibodies to confirm AS-FcRγ co-immunoprecipitation with and support of receptor α-chain expression in transfection systems and primary cells. We assessed the function of the AS-FcRγ isoform by stimulus-induced cytokine production and degranulation. In the human genome, insertions, deletions and rearrangements of FCER1G are absent, and with the exception of very rare single nucleotide variants, the FcRγ protein is monomorphic. Surprisingly, we confirmed that an alternatively spliced (AS) form of FcRγ message encodes a translated protein (AS-FcRγ) expressed in human myeloid cells. AS-FcRγ pairs with ligand binding FcR α-chains. The alternate exon 5' in AS-FcRγ creates a novel cytoplasmic domain with a disrupted ITAM motif. Co-immunoprecipitation showed that AS-FcRγ associates with FcαRI in circulating neutrophils and mononuclear cells. A chimeric molecule consisting of the extracellular domain of FcαRI fused to the cytoplasmic domain of AS-FcRγ fails to stimulate cellular degranulation and cytokine production. AS-FcRγ is an expressed protein that associates with partner alpha-chains but is not signaling competent. It may represent a novel contributory mechanism mitigating the ability of Fc receptors to stimulate cellular signaling in myeloid cells with important implications for host defense and antibody-mediated autoimmune diseases.

title: Methylglyoxal hampers the angiogenic capacity of human retinal endothelial cells modifying cell transcriptome with the contribution of NRSF/REST.
abstract: The functional impairment of retinal microvascular cells is an early and central event in diabetic retinopathy (DR). Methylglyoxal (MGO), the most reactive precursor of advanced glycation end products (AGEs), has been implicated in vascular injury and neuro-retinal dysfunction. Its direct effects on retinal endothelial cells and underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Human retinal endothelial cells (hRECs) were exposed to MGO and the effect of sublethal doses on the proangiogenic function was evaluated by migration, tube formation and pericyte recruitment assays. MGO derived AGEs were evaluated by western blot. Transcriptome and miRNome profiling were performed to identify gene expression and microRNA perturbations. Integrative in silico analyses combining RNA-Seq with ENCODE ChIP-Seq datasets were used to identify transcriptional regulators responsible for MGO-induced gene deregulation. Transcriptomic profiles were compared with independent human DR datasets, and REST was silenced by siRNAs followed by analyses of proangiogenic function. The exposure of hRECs to MGO for 72 h is sufficient to increase protein glycation adducts, impair the migration, tube-formation and the recruitment of pericytes. Transcriptome and miRNome analyses highlight that MGO induces extensive transcriptional perturbations, related to gene expression regulation, cell cycle, cell death and vasculature development. Among the identified transcriptional regulators, Neuron-Restrictive Silencer Factor/RE1-Silencing Transcription Factor (NRSF/REST) emerges as a candidate mediator, with binding sites enriched in 56% of deregulated genes. NRSF/REST expression markedly increases after 24 h of MGO treatment, suggesting it is an early event of the exposure to MGO. Protein-protein interaction network analysis prioritized NRSF/REST as a central node linking key MGO-responsive pathways. Accordingly, NRSF/REST knockdown is associated with the reduction of TP53 and FOSL2, which are induced by MGO and display NRSF binding sites and known migration-related functions. Importantly, REST silencing significantly attenuates MGO-induced defects in endothelial migration, tube formation and pericyte recruitment, supporting its contribution to both transcriptional and functional endothelial alterations induced by MGO in hRECs. These findings demonstrate that MGO exposure disrupts endothelial function and transcriptional homeostasis in hRECs, identifying NRSF/REST as a contributor to MGO-induced endothelial dysfunction and supporting further investigations of the MGO/NRSF-REST axis as a potential therapeutic target for DR.

title: RNA N6-methyladenosine modifications in plants: molecular mechanisms and biological roles.
abstract: RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications dynamically modulate RNA stability, splicing, and translation in plants, influencing developmental and stress response processes. In this review, we provide an overview of the key protein complexes involved in RNA m6A modification, including methyltransferases, demethylases, and m6A-binding proteins. We then demonstrate that m6A modulates vegetative growth, reproductive processes, responses to stresses, and hormone signaling. In agronomically important crops, RNA m6A modifications affect stress resilience, developmental timing, and quality traits, such as drought tolerance, salt resistance, male fertility, pollen viability, and fruit maturation. Furthermore, we elucidate the molecular mechanisms of RNA m6A. Finally, we explore advancements in m6A detection technologies, highlighting emerging trends and future directions. These strategies provide a conceptual framework for moving plant m6A research from descriptive epitranscriptomics toward trait-oriented crop and forest tree improvement.

title: Enhancing Proliferation and Pluripotency in Human Dental Pulp Stem Cells through 980-nm Laser Irradiation: Implications for Regenerative Dentistry.
abstract: Introduction: Dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) possess remarkable proliferative ability and multilineage differentiation potential, and they are known as immunomodulatory cells. Identifying factors that enhance DPSC proliferation is crucial, as accelerated expansion is necessary for tissue engineering applications, while maintaining pluripotency gene expression is essential to preserve their proliferative and differentiation potential. Low-level laser irradiation (LLLI) has increasingly been recognized as a promising non-invasive approach to accelerate proliferation and enhance tissue regeneration. Within this framework, the current study was designed to evaluate the influence of laser irradiation on proliferation, pluripotency, and angiogenesis in DPSCs. Methods: The DPSCs were purchased from the Iranian Biological Resources Center and cultured under standard conditions. The experimental protocol involved exposing DPSCs to a 980 nm diode laser with an output power of 50 mW for a duration of 20 seconds, corresponding to an energy density of 1 J/cm2. Following a 24-hour incubation period post-irradiation, cell viability was quantitatively measured using the MTT colorimetric assay. Subsequently, the expression levels of Sox2, Nanog, VEGF, TGF-β, PCNA, and Cyclin D1 were assessed through quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), while the protein expression of Sox2, TGF-β, and Cyclin D1 was determined using western blot analysis. Results: The results showed that laser irradiation at 980 nm for 20 seconds increased the expression of Sox2, TGF-β, and Cyclin D1 at the RNA expression level (P<0.05). Moreover, Sox2 and Cyclin D1 protein levels were increased compared to the control group. Conclusion: Our findings suggest that irradiation with a 980-nm laser at an energy density of 1 J/cm2 significantly enhances the proliferative capacity and upregulates pluripotency marker expression in DPSCs, supporting its potential as a therapeutic approach in regenerative medicine.

title: Harnessing double-stranded RNA therapy targeting coat protein (CP), helper component-protease (HC-Pro) and viral protein genome-linked (VPg) for controlling chilli veinal mottle virus in Capsicum chinense cv. Umorok.
abstract: Chilli is an economically and culturally important crop, particularly in Northeast India, where indigenous cultivars such as Capsicum chinense cv. Umorok support smallholder livelihoods and regional agrobiodiversity. However, its productivity is severely constrained by viral diseases, among which chilli veinal mottle virus (ChiVMV) is a major limiting factor. Conventional management strategies are largely ineffective, often relying on chemical inputs that pose environmental risks and fail to provide durable protection, especially under mixed infection scenarios. RNA interference, mediated by double-stranded RNA, offers a highly specific, environmentally safe, eco-friendly pest management alternative, adaptable to targeting essential viral genes. The present study evaluates the efficacy of exogenously applied dsRNAs targeting key genes of ChiVMV: coat protein, helper component-protease and viral protein genome-linked, in suppressing viral infection. dsRNAs were produced using the E. coli HT115(DE3) expression system, yielding 10-15 mg/mL of purified product. Disease progression was assessed across three greenhouse trials using a 0-4 disease rating scale, with disease severity index ranging from 25 to 75%. All dsRNA treatments significantly reduced viral RNA accumulation and delayed symptom development compared to untreated controls. The multitarget construct (dsTotal) exhibited the highest antiviral efficacy, maintaining substantially lower viral loads (8.79-fold change) relative to controls (1761.32-fold) at 20 days post-treatment. This enhanced performance is attributed to the simultaneous disruption of viral replication, suppression of host RNA silencing, and virion assembly. These findings demonstrate that multi-gene dsRNA-based RNAi provides a robust and sustainable strategy for managing ChiVMV, highlighting its potential as a superior alternative to conventional approaches for virus control in chilli cultivation. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12298-026-01814-3.

title: Detection of the RNA-Editing Enzyme ADARB1 in Primary Auditory Neurons and Anti-ADARB1 Immunofluorescence as a Means for Automated Counting.
abstract: Spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), the primary auditory afferents in the inner ear, are vulnerable to degeneration from neuropathies, concussion, and aging, among other causes. Accurate quantification of SGNs is critical for assessing degeneration and therapeutic interventions, but manual counting is arduous due to dense cellular crowding and unreliable nuclear markers. Because SGNs receive input from GluA2-containing AMPA receptors, the transcripts for which must be RNA-edited for calcium impermeability, we hypothesized that SGNs express high levels of the RNA-editing enzyme ADARB1. Here, we confirm enriched expression of Adarb1 transcripts in SGNs and show that anti-ADARB1 antibodies robustly label the nuclei of type I and type II SGNs from young and aged mice, adult macaques, and adult humans. Neuronal versus glial specificity was confirmed using antibodies against neurofilament heavy chain (NFH), human antigen D (HuD), GATA binding protein 3 (GATA3), and SRY-box 2 (SOX2). A blinded investigator manually counted mouse SGNs via NFH, and these were compared to automated counts of ADARB1-positive nuclei using the analyze particles function in ImageJ. A concordance correlation coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated strong agreement between the manual and automated counts. Together, these results suggest broad utility of ADARB1 immunolabeling for automated counts of SGNs across species.

title: Multi-omics insight into cardiac myofibril remodeling in post-prandial Burmese pythons.
abstract: Burmese pythons exhibit cardiac remodeling in response to increased metabolic rate during digestion. Here, we performed single-myofibril mechanics measurements and myosin biochemical assays to evaluate the impact of feeding on the cardiomyocyte sarcomere in two experimental paradigms: normal feeding (one meal per month) and frequent feeding (eight meals per month). Myofibril tension and rate of relaxation increased during digestion in both paradigms, while frequent feeding was further associated with slower myofibril activation. To gain potential mechanistic insight, we performed multi-omics analyses. RNA sequencing identified increased relative concentration of some sarcomeric mRNAs during digestion; however, proteomics suggested a delay in sarcomere protein synthesis at the peak of remodeling, as the relative abundance of most sarcomere proteins declined. Analysis of post-translational modifications identified hundreds of sites on sarcomere proteins, including on the tension-regulating proteins titin and myosin. Our results detail the molecular underpinnings of cardiac remodeling in digesting Burmese pythons and suggest the mechanism for rapidly increasing myofibril function is a post-translational program.

title: Context-dependent protective and pathogenic functions of YTHDF1 in MASLD and hepatocellular carcinoma: Mechanisms and design of therapeutics.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most common chronic liver disease and can progressively develop into inflammatory metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and liver fibrosis. During this progression, activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) leads to excessive accumulation of extracellular matrix. There is a growing trend to develop into hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The limited availability of effective therapeutics highlights the need to better understand the underlying pathogenic mechanisms. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is a key post-transcriptional RNA modification that regulates gene expression and governs a broad range of physiological and pathological processes. YTH domain family 1 (YTHDF1) is a reader protein that recognizes m6A modifications on mRNAs and enhances their stability or translation by interacting with key components of the translation machinery. YTHDF1 exhibits context-dependent functions in MASLD and liver fibrosis, while it promotes HCC pathogenesis. Hepatocytic YTHDF1 alleviates MASLD by improving mitochondrial function, serving as a protective factor during its early stages. YTHDF1 in HSCs is important for initiating liver fibrosis, yet it also plays a crucial role in regulating HSC ferroptosis to counteract established fibrosis. Our structure-based analyses of YTHDF1 inhibitors reveal novel concepts, including inhibition of YTHDF1-induced condensates and direct degradation of YTHDF1 proteins by fullerene derivatives and metal-organic frameworks. YTHDF1 inhibitors serve as selective chemical probes for interrogating YTHDF1's cell type-specific functions in MASLD. They are also promising candidates for in vivo evaluation to treat MASLD and HCC and to prevent liver fibrosis at early stages.

title: Shortening of the Zfp143 3'UTR by alternative polyadenylation alters ZFP36L1-mediated regulation and promotes adipogenesis.
abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms governing adipogenesis is essential for elucidating adipose tissue development and metabolic disorders. Alternative polyadenylation (APA) of the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) has emerged as an important regulatory layer in adipogenesis; however, the functional significance of APA-induced 3'UTR shortening in individual genes remains to be elucidated. This study aimed to investigate the roles and mechanisms of APA-generated zinc-finger protein 143 (Zfp143) isoforms in adipogenesis. The expression pattern of Zfp143 during adipogenesis was characterized, and functional analyses revealed the involvement of Zfp143 in adipogenic differentiation. Using 3'RACE, two Zfp143 isoforms with long and short 3'UTRs were identified. To evaluate the functional differences between APA-generated isoforms, isoform-specific expression constructs containing the identical Zfp143 coding sequence fused with either the short or long 3'UTR were generated. The short 3'UTR isoform exhibited higher Zfp143 expression levels and stronger adipogenic capacity than the long isoform. Dual-luciferase reporter assays, RNA immunoprecipitation assays, and molecular analyses demonstrated differential post-transcriptional regulation between the two isoforms. Mechanistically, the long 3'UTR isoform was negatively regulated by ZFP36L1 binding to AREs within its 3'UTR, whereas the short isoform escaped ZFP36L1-mediated regulation due to the absence of AREs in its 3'UTR. Collectively, these findings reveal an APA-dependent post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism in which ZFP36L1 differentially regulates Zfp143 3'UTR isoforms, thereby fine-tuning Zfp143 expression and adipogenic differentiation during adipogenesis.

title: Structurally diverse polyprenylated acylphloroglucinols from Hypericum addingtonii with anti-hepatocellular carcinoma activity.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. In this study, 40 benzoylated polycyclic polyprenylated acylphloroglucinols (PPAPs), including 11 new compounds, hyperadditionciols A-K (1-11), were isolated from the fruits of Hypericum addingtonii. Compounds 1-40 were classified into bicyclo[3.3.1]nonane, adamantane, homo-adamantane, 1,2-seco, and complex PPAPs. The structures of 1-11 were established by HRESIMS and 1D and 2D NMR spectroscopic analyses, while their stereochemical assignments were supported by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, ECD calculations, and GIAO NMR calculations. Compounds 2, 3, and 5-40 were evaluated for cytotoxicity against HepG2 cells, and selected active compounds were further tested against Huh7 cells, with several PPAPs showing cytotoxicity against both cell lines. Subsequent SPR screening showed that hyperisampsin J (15) directly bound to DEAD-box RNA helicase 5 (DDX5), with a KD value of 5.02 μM. Molecular docking and a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation supported the plausibility and stability of the predicted binding mode. Western blot analysis further showed increased DDX5 and decreased p62/sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1) protein levels in HepG2 cells following treatment with 15. These findings expand the chemical diversity of benzoylated PPAPs from H. addingtonii and support further investigation of this class of natural products for their potential anti-HCC activity.

title: The complete chloroplast genome of Erigeron sumatrensis (Asteraceae): genomic features and phylogenetic implications.
abstract: Erigeron sumatrensis Retz. (Asteraceae) is an annual herb native to South America that has become a noxious invasive weed in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. Here, we report the first complete chloroplast genome of this plant species. The chloroplast genome is 152,974 bp in length and exhibits a typical quadripartite structure, consisting of a large single-copy (LSC) region of 84,615 bp, a small single-copy (SSC) region of 18,335 bp, and a pair of inverted repeat (IR) regions of 25,012 bp each. The overall GC content is 37.16%. The genome encodes 133 genes, including 88 protein-coding genes, 37 transfer RNA (tRNA) genes, and 8 ribosomal RNA (rRNA) genes. Phylogenetic analysis based on 29 chloroplast genomes indicated its close affinity to E. rupicola and E. fernandezianus within Erigeron. This study provides an important genomic resource for species identification, population genetics, and research on the invasion mechanism of E. sumatrensis.

title: Ribosomal RNA operon copy number: A trait-informed framework to close the microbial cultivation gap.
abstract: The vast majority of microbes remain uncultured, constraining functional validation and limiting microbiome-based applications. We show that ribosomal RNA operon (rrn) copy number-a stable, phylogenetically conserved genomic trait-is strongly correlated with cultivation outcomes across ecosystems. Comparative analyses of rhizosphere, human gut, and mouse gut microbiomes reveal that rhizosphere communities contain a higher proportion of high-rrn taxa, which are preferentially recovered under nutrient-rich, short-term cultivation, whereas low-rrn taxa are systematically underrepresented. By linking rrn distributions to cultivation success, we propose trait-informed strategies for media design, incubation regimes, co-culture approaches, and preservation methods. This framework provides a predictive, generalizable path to bridge sequencing and cultivation, facilitating biodiversity conservation, sustainable agriculture, and microbiome-based therapeutics.

title: Congenital hyperinsulinism as part of a multisystem disease caused by a compound heterozygous variant in the YARS1 gene.
abstract: Tyrosyl-transfer RNA (tRNA) synthetase, encoded by YARS1, is essential for protein synthesis, catalyzing the attachment of tyrosine to its cognate tRNA during translation. Pathogenic biallelic YARS1 variants cause infantile-onset multisystem neurological, endocrine, and pancreatic disease type 2 (IMNEPD2; OMIM #619418), an orphan disorder. Hypoglycemia in IMNEPD2 remains poorly characterized, with few reported cases. We describe an infant with a compound heterozygous YARS1 genotype (c.176T>C and c.1261G>A) who presented with severe hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, notable for a discordance between insulin and C-peptide concentrations and a lack of response to diazoxide and octreotide.

title: A Data-Centric Diagnostic Framework for Experimental Design and Mechanistic Modeling: Application to mRNA Production.
abstract: In this study, we present a data-centric framework for the integrated investigation of experimental behavior and mechanistic model performance in complex biochemical systems. The framework is demonstrated on the in vitro transcription (IVT) reaction for mRNA production. Rather than analyzing experimental data and mechanistic models independently, the framework links experimental-response surrogate modeling, a surrogate model of error characterizing model-experiment discrepancy, and mechanistic parameter sensitivity within a unified workflow. Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) and Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA) are first used to interrogate experimental data, identify statistically anomalous observations, and characterize the process variables and interactions governing the response. Predictions from the resulting experimental-response surrogate are then compared with those of an existing mechanistic model, and the resulting discrepancy is represented through a surrogate model of error and subjected to GSA. Finally, the process-level drivers of this discrepancy are cross-compared with sensitivities of the mechanistic kinetic parameters, thereby linking experimental and mechanistic information to prioritize subsequent investigation. The experimental-response surrogate achieved an R 2 of 0.90, with MgOAc and NTP concentrations dominating variation in mRNA yield and incubation time contributing principally through interactions. The surrogate model of error achieved an R 2 of 0.86 and identified NTP, MgOAc, T7-RNA polymerase, and selected interactions as the principal contributors to the discrepancy between mechanistic and experimental-surrogate predictions. Cross-comparison with mechanistic parameter sensitivities subsequently prioritized the Mg degradation rate constant (k Mg ), DNA equilibrium constant (K DNA ), Mg saturation constant (k 1), and transcription rate constant (k app ), together with their associated model components, for further investigation. The resulting framework provides a systematic basis for directing subsequent repeat or targeted experimentation, parameter recalibration, and structural model refinement.

title: Proteomic profiling of high purity extracellular vesicle subtypes from megakaryoblastic leukemia cells provides insights into myeloproliferative neoplasm biology.
abstract: Aim: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are emerging as important mediators in myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), but the characteristics of distinct EV subtypes remain unclear. This study aimed to characterize the molecular heterogeneity of MEG-01-derived large EVs (lEVs) and small EVs (sEVs). Methods: lEVs and sEVs were isolated from MEG-01 cell culture medium by differential centrifugation followed by density gradient ultracentrifugation. EVs were characterized by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, immunoblotting, and on-bead flow cytometry. Quantitative proteomic analysis was performed to compare the protein cargo of lEVs and sEVs, followed by Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses. Results: Density gradient purification yielded high purity of lEV and sEV with distinct size, morphologies, and protein compositions. On-bead flow cytometry enabled efficient profiling of EV surface markers. Proteomic analysis revealed a shared core proteome between lEVs and sEVs, together with subtype specific protein signatures. Enrichment analyses indicated distinct molecular characteristics of the two EV populations, with sEVs showing enrichment of proteins associated with RNA-related processes and vesicle-mediated transport, whereas lEVs were enriched in proteins related to cytoskeletal organization and metabolism. Conclusion: MEG-01 derived lEVs and sEVs comprise molecularly distinct subpopulations with shared and subtype specific protein cargo. The workflow established in this study provides a robust platform for high purity EV isolation and characterization, and offers insights into MEG-01 EV heterogeneity relevant to megakaryocyte biology and MPN research.

title: Toxicological Vulnerabilities and Emerging Safety Signals in Modified mRNA Vaccine Technology: A Narrative Review of the COVID-19 Experience.
abstract: The rapid deployment in early 2021 of modified mRNA (modRNA) as a vaccine platform for the COVID-19 pandemic sparked a wave of optimism for its potential as a preventive medicine. However, this compacted timeframe may not have fully addressed certain toxicological risks associated with this new technology, which would typically require more extensive preclinical testing. Five years postrollout, an accumulating body of postauthorisation evidence has highlighted safety signals that require closer scrutiny, such as those concerning biodistribution, off-target effects and persistent adverse events. Independent analyses of Phase III trial data and pharmacovigilance reports have raised questions regarding benefit-risk balance and potential long-term biological effects. This narrative review examines the evolution of the toxicological understanding of modified RNA as a vaccine technology from platform design through long-term observational data, identifying areas of uncertainty and vulnerability that may inform future development and regulatory evaluation. The review emphasises that fast-tracked decision-making under exceptional uncertainty requires explicit safeguards to prevent premature certainty and to support learning from emerging evidence over time.

title: High-throughput screening to identify inhibitors of the MTB CARD•RNA polymerase protein-protein interaction.
abstract: In 2023, tuberculosis (TB) once again became the world's deadliest infectious disease, overtaking COVID-19 as the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB). The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that the COVID-19 pandemic has reversed years of progress in providing essential TB services and reducing TB disease burden. In 2025, TB was responsible for an estimated 1.23 million deaths globally (95% uncertainty interval: 1.13-1.33 million), and there were 400 K cases of rifamycin resistant/multidrug resistant TB (RR, RIFR, MDR). While treatment success for drug susceptible TB remains high (88%), outcomes for MDR/RR-TB are lower but improving, reaching 71% globally. Clearly, there is a critical unmet need for novel antibiotics against MTB, exacerbated now due to COVID-19. The limited success in pursuing novel targets underscores the urgent need to revisit and reevaluate the mechanisms of action behind existing and once effective drugs, a strategy that may hold untapped potential in the fight against growing antibiotic-resistant TB. The MTB RNA polymerase (RNAP) is a proven target for TB treatment by rifampin (RMP), which kills both active and latent MTB. However, RMP suffers from several drawbacks including: long treatment times, activation of hPXR (inducing Cyp3A4 which is problematic for HIV-TB coinfection), and resistant mutations within RNAP. Two newer treatments with novel mechanisms of action include bedaquiline and delamanid, the former has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of multiple-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-MTB); however, even these new drugs already have incidences of acquired resistance. Our goal is to develop novel drug candidates for TB treatment that: target RNAP, have the potential to shorten treatment times, and have activity against RIFR mutants. Our approach, orthogonal to the rifamycins, is to target the interaction of MTB RNAP with the required transcription factor CarD. We have previously labeled CarD with the BODIPY-FL fluorophore via engineered cysteine mutations and developed a fluorescence polarization assay to monitor its interaction with RNAP and promoter DNA. Leveraging this target, we screened a 24 K small molecule library against CarD binding to MTB RNAP. We have now extended this screening to∼88,000 additional molecules.

title: Machine learning method for optimizing coding sequences in mammalian cells.
abstract: Mammalian cell lines are the preferred hosts for producing commercially relevant therapeutic proteins such as antibodies, antibody derivatives, and cytokine fusion proteins. Even though significant investment is made to optimize upstream and downstream processes, the optimal gene design parameters for heterologous recombinant protein expression remain poorly understood. We describe a generic approach to gene optimization in which design features are systematically sampled and iteratively modulated using machine learning (ML). Synthetic gene variants encoding the Dasher fluorescent protein, differing only in synonymous codons, were used to interrogate the gene-sequence preferences of transient antibody-expressing HEK293 cells. Synonymous codon variations influenced expression by more than 2 orders of magnitude. This variation in protein yield was used to build ML models relating gene design features, which were then employed to design further-improved genes. The ML models were shown to be expression system-specific. Messenger RNA levels and ribosome occupancy were highly correlated with protein levels, suggesting that mRNA lifetime is influenced by coding bias. Our results illustrate a novel, generally applicable method to improve gene expression via synonymous re-coding for any protein target or host cell.

title: DNA oligonucleotides encoding suppressor tRNA induce readthrough of premature termination codon.
abstract: Nonsense mutation is a type of DNA mutation that converts sense codon in mRNA into premature termination codon (PTC), causing protein truncation. Recent studies have revealed that suppressor tRNAs, which read the stop codon instead of the natural codon and encode the desired amino acid, induce PTC readthrough and restore protein function. However, RNA is prone to degradation, presenting numerous challenges for tissue delivery in gene therapy. Here, we show that DNA oligonucleotides encoding suppressor tRNA sequences but without additional Pol III promoters induce PTC readthrough in cultured cells. Sequence-matched microRNAs specifically inhibited PTC readthrough mediated by the transfected DNA oligonucleotides. Furthermore, treatment with an RNA Pol III inhibitor significantly reduced DNA oligonucleotide-mediated PTC readthrough. These findings support the conclusion that functional suppressor tRNAs are transcribed from DNA oligonucleotides in cultured cells. These results suggest that DNA oligonucleotides hold potential as a novel therapeutic approach enabling suppressor tRNA expression for nonsense mutation repair.

title: Evaluating Plasma-Handling Effects on Extracellular Vesicle RNA Yield and Cargo Profiles in Fish: A Methodological Insight.
abstract: Extracellular vesicle (EV)-derived RNA (EV-RNA) is emerging as a valuable biomarker source in aquatic species. However, the composition and stability of long RNA species, particularly messenger RNA (mRNAs) and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), remain largely unexplored in teleosts. Pre-analytical factors such as input plasma volume and storage conditions may influence RNA recovery, especially in low-input samples like fish plasma. Here, we evaluated the effects of input sample volume and freezing storage on EV-RNA yield and integrity in gilthead sea bream (Sparus aurata) plasma using the exoRNeasy commercial kit. Both Maxi (∼2 mL) and Midi (∼1 mL) kit formats produced comparable RNA recovery, indicating flexibility in plasma volume requirements. Freezing did not alter the overall RNA biotype composition or the identity of the dominant transcripts but resulted in a higher proportion of shorter and incomplete isoforms, suggesting selective susceptibility to degradation of long RNAs during freezing storage. Using Oxford Nanopore Technologies long-read sequencing, we generated the first long RNA-resolved EV transcriptome for this species. EV cargo was dominated by ribosomal and metabolic mRNAs, consistent with conserved vertebrate EV signatures, and 302 distinct lncRNAs were identified, two of which accounted for nearly 90% of lncRNA reads. Predicted interactions between abundant lncRNAs, EV mRNAs, and their encoded ribonucleoproteins suggest coordinated packaging of RNA-protein modules. Overall, this study validates exoRNeasy for fish plasma and provides the first comprehensive long-RNA EV landscape in a teleost, providing a valuable framework for future molecular and functional studies in non-model fish species.

title: Artificial intelligence in spatial transcriptomics: a review of methods, datasets, and directions.
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (STs) measures gene expression while retaining the location of transcripts or cells within tissue sections. Unlike bulk RNA sequencing, which averages expression across cell populations, and single-cell RNA sequencing, which generally requires tissue dissociation, ST links molecular profiles to tissue architecture. This spatial information supports the analysis of tissue heterogeneity, cellular organization, and potential intercellular interactions. The spatially resolved nature of ST has unlocked diverse applications in fields such as cancer, neuroscience, reproductive biology, and plant biology. In parallel, the development of publicly accessible databases and repositories has facilitated large-scale, multi-cohort comparisons and benchmarking. The rapid expansion and increasing complexity of these datasets have driven the adoption of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques. These computational tools support a range of tasks, including data pre-processing, image segmentation, spatial domain identification, and pattern recognition. Moreover, they are instrumental in integrative multi-omics analyses and predictive modeling. This AI-focused review provides necessary background on ST technologies and databases and evaluates the use of statistical, ML, and DL methods across the analytical workflow, from image and sequencing-data preprocessing to spatial analysis and LLM-assisted interpretation. We compile key resources related to datasets, AI-driven analytical frameworks, and ST data analysis pipelines, and discuss current challenges, limitations, and future directions for AI-based tools in spatial omics.

title: BBOX1-AS1 mediates Lenvatinib resistance through IGF2BP1-dependent MYC mRNA stabilization.
abstract: Lenvatinib is a standard first-line treatment for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, acquired lenvatinib resistance remains a major challenge. Here, we identify BBOX1-AS1 as a new mediator of lenvatinib resistance in HCC. BBOX1-AS1 is markedly upregulated in lenvatinib-resistant HCC cell lines and in tumor specimens from patients who progressed during lenvatinib treatment. Lower BBOX1-AS1 expression was associated with significantly longer progression-free survival (median PFS, 8 vs 3.7 months; P = 0.0041). Furthermore, knockdown of BBOX1-AS1 restored lenvatinib sensitivity in both cell and xenograft models. Mechanistically, BBOX1-AS1 binds the RNA-binding protein IGF2BP1 and promotes its recruitment to MYC mRNA, stabilizing the transcript, elevating c-Myc protein, and activating AKT signaling. Actinomycin D chase assays and IGF2BP1 knockdown experiments further established that BBOX1-AS1-mediated MYC mRNA stabilization is dependent on IGF2BP1. These findings indicate that the BBOX1-AS1/IGF2BP1/c-Myc axis contributes to lenvatinib resistance in HCC. BBOX1-AS1 may serve as a biomarker for lenvatinib response and a potential therapeutic target in resistant HCC.

title: CircUGP2 inhibits tumor progression via PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling through sponging miR-137-3p and interacting with UPF1 in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Circular RNA (circRNA) has been shown to have a pivotal role in the initiation and evolution of multiple tumors, but its function in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) requires further elucidation. circUGP2 (hsa_circ_0001020) was identified in the GEO database by HCC circRNA microarray. Subsequently, an assessment was conducted to determine the biological effects of circUGP2, employing a series of analytical methods, including CCK8, EdU, colony formation, transwell, scratch assays, and in vivo experimentation. To explore the functions of circUGP2 as a sponge, including RNA pull-down, microRNA-seq, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), and luciferase reporter assays were employed. Mass spectrometry (MS), RIP, and co-inmunoprecipitation (Co-IP) were employed to examine the interaction between cirrcUGP2 and up-frameshift protein 1 (UPF1). circUGP2 was downregulated in HCC tissues and cells, which inhibited the growth and spread of HCC in vitro and in vivo. In the mechanisms, circUGP2 has the capacity to modulate KLF4 by sponging miR-137-3p, thereby suppressing HCC growth and migration. In addition, circUGP2 could combine with UPF1 and facilitate an interplay between UPF1 and AKT, influencing tumor progression in HCC via inactivation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. circUGP2 has a crucial function in HCC development by modulating the miR-137-3p/KLF4 axis to inactivate the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway and by interacting with UPF1. The findings indicate the potential of circUGP2 as a novel biomarker and target for HCC.

title: hsa_circ_0001377 promotes hepatic fibrosis by sponging let-7a-5p and targeting TGFBR1, Smad2, and Col1a2.
abstract: Background: Hepatic fibrosis (HF) is primarily driven by the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) and is characterized by excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have recently gained increasing attention in HF research. Methods: RNA sequencing and bioinformatic analyses revealed elevated hsa_circ_0001377 expression in human HF tissues. Its circular structure and subcellular localization were identified using Sanger sequencing, RNase R treatment, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Gain- and loss-of-function experiments were conducted to elucidate the role of hsa_circ_0001377 in the human HSC line LX-2. Furthermore, the in vitro and in vivo effects of the hsa_circ_0001377/let-7a-5p/TGFBR1, Smad2, and Col1a2 regulatory axis were investigated using cytological assays and a bile duct ligation (BDL)-induced mouse model of HF. Results: hsa_circ_0001377 was significantly upregulated in the circRNA expression profile of human HF tissues. Its circular structure was validated through Sanger sequencing and resistance to RNase R digestion. FISH and co-staining with α-SMA demonstrated that hsa_circ_0001377 was abundantly expressed in activated HSCs (aHSCs; α-SMA-positive cells). Gain- and loss-of-function assays were performed using LX-2 cells with stable hsa_circ_0001377 overexpression and a specific siRNA targeting this circRNA. hsa_circ_0001377 overexpression promoted LX-2 cell activation, proliferation, migration, and G1/S-phase transition, whereas its knockdown produced the opposite effects. qRT-PCR, AGO-RIP, dual-luciferase reporter, and miRNA pulldown assays confirmed that hsa_circ_0001377 acts as a molecular sponge for let-7a-5p and that let-7a-5p targets TGFBR1, Smad2, and Col1a2. Rescue experiments in LX-2 cells further demonstrated that hsa_circ_0001377 promotes HSC activation, proliferation, migration, and G1/S-phase transition through the let-7a-5p/TGFBR1, Smad2, and Col1a2 axis. Moreover, hsa_circ_0001377 was highly expressed in 20 human HF samples, and its expression increased with advancing fibrosis stage. In vivo, a BDL-induced murine HF model demonstrated that the homologous mmu_circ_0001377 was also significantly upregulated in fibrotic liver tissues. In addition, tail-vein injection of an mmu-let-7a-5p agomir into BDL-induced HF mice confirmed the inhibitory effects of the let-7a-5p/TGFBR1, Smad2, and Col1a2 axis on α-SMA expression and collagen deposition. Conclusion: Taken together, these findings suggest that the hsa_circ_0001377/let-7a-5p/TGFBR1, Smad2, and Col1a2 regulatory axis may represent a promising therapeutic target for HF.

title: Extracellular vesicle-delivered siRNA targeting RCN1 suppresses acute myeloid leukemia through TFAM-dependent mtDNA-cGAS-STING signaling.
abstract: Aim: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains a highly aggressive hematologic malignancy with limited therapeutic options. This study aimed to elucidate how reticulocalbin-1 (RCN1) regulates mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)-mediated innate immune signaling in AML and to evaluate the therapeutic potential of extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated small interfering RNA (siRNA) delivery targeting RCN1. Methods: Stable RCN1 knockdown was achieved in AML cells using lentiviral delivery of short hairpin RNA. Mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) expression, mtDNA leakage, and activation of the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING)-type I interferon pathway were analyzed by immunoblotting and quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Protein interactions were assessed by co-immunoprecipitation, proximity ligation assay, and immunofluorescence. TFAM rescue experiments were performed to evaluate its contribution to the downstream effects of RCN1 knockdown. For translational evaluation, EVs were isolated and characterized by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and marker protein detection, followed by loading with siRNA targeting RCN1. Therapeutic efficacy and safety were assessed in an AML xenograft mouse model. Results: RCN1 knockdown reduced TFAM expression, leading to cytoplasmic mtDNA accumulation and activation of the cGAS-STING-type I interferon signaling pathway. Restoration of TFAM expression attenuated mtDNA leakage and downstream signaling. EV-delivered siRCN1 effectively suppressed tumor growth in vivo without detectable toxicity. Conclusion: RCN1 silencing destabilizes mtDNA integrity and activates innate immune signaling in AML. EV-based delivery of siRCN1 may represent a promising and potentially safe therapeutic strategy for AML.

title: hnRNPC promotes oral squamous cell carcinoma progression via N6-methyladenosine-dependent stabilization of BCAT1 to enhance branched-chain amino acid metabolism.
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains a major cause of cancer-associated mortality worldwide, with current treatments limited by chemoresistance and long-term toxicities. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification regulates mRNA fate to drive cancer progression. However, how m6A modification regulates OSCC progression remains to be elucidated. The present study integrated bioinformatics analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas and Genotype-Tissue Expression datasets and experimental validation to explore the role of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C (hnRNPC), an m6A-associated RNA-binding protein, in OSCC. Bioinformatics analysis of 515 patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) suggested that hnRNPC may have prognostic relevance in HNSCC. High hnRNPC expression associated with advanced pathological stages, poor overall survival and served as a potential risk factor for HNSCC. Functional experiments demonstrated that hnRNPC knockdown in OSCC cell lines inhibited cell proliferation, colony formation, tumor sphere formation and in vivo tumor growth, while downregulating stemness-associated genes (Oct4, Sox2 and Nanog). Mechanistically, hnRNPC promoted branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) metabolism in OSCC. High hnRNPC expression was associated with activated BCAA metabolic pathways and hnRNPC knockdown reduced BCAA uptake, glutamate levels, oxygen consumption rate and glutathione levels. Furthermore, hnRNPC stabilized BCCAA transaminase 1 (BCAT1) mRNA in an m6A-dependent manner. BCAT1 inhibition via ERG240 enhanced the tumor-suppressive effects of hnRNPC knockdown. Exogenous supplementation of α-ketoglutarate rescued energy deficiency and functional defects in hnRNPC-knockdown OSCC cells. Collectively, the present study findings revealed a novel mechanism driving OSCC progression. In this mechanism, hnRNPC regulates BCAA metabolism by stabilizing BCAT1 mRNA in an m6A-dependent manner. The present study supports the prognostic relevance of hnRNPC and may offer a promising therapeutic direction in improving OSCC treatment outcomes by disrupting tumor-specific metabolic and epigenetic adaptations.

title: The ncRNA-Epigenetic-Cuproptosis Axis in Liver Diseases: From Copper Homeostasis to Precision Hepatology.
abstract: Cuproptosis, a recently defined copper-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by excess intracellular copper, is characterized by copper binding to lipoylated tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle proteins, causing aberrant protein oligomerization, iron-sulfur cluster loss, and proteotoxic stress. Given the liver's central role in copper homeostasis, hepatocytes are particularly vulnerable to this death modality. This review examines the emerging non-coding RNA (ncRNA)-epigenetic-cuproptosis axis in liver diseases, critically evaluating the evidence across a spectrum from well-established biochemical principles to largely hypothetical connections. Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications, can modulate cuproptosis sensitivity. The methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3)-m6A- fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1)-ferredoxin 1 (FDX1) axis, which confers cuproptosis resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) through translational repression of FDX1, represents the strongest mechanistic evidence in hepatic contexts. ncRNAs, including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), and circular RNAs (circRNAs), add additional regulatory layers; miR-133a-5p has been shown to facilitate cuproptosis in hepatocellular carcinoma by targeting ATP7B. We additionally highlight high-copper HCC phenotypes, the MYC-CTR1 and COMMD3 pro-tumor axes, and ferroptosis-cuproptosis combination strategies as priority translational directions. We systematically evaluate the ncRNA-epigenetic-cuproptosis axis across major liver diseases, including metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease, alcohol-associated liver disease, viral hepatitis, cholestatic liver disease, hepatic fibrosis, ischemia-reperfusion injury, Wilson disease, and HCC. Evidence tiers range from direct functional validation, such as copper ionophore-induced cuproptosis in HCC cells and cholestatic liver injury models, through promising but incomplete data, to largely bioinformatic associations lacking functional validation. Translational opportunities include biomarker development, copper ionophore-based therapeutics, and ncRNA-targeted interventions; we further distinguish mechanistic evidence from available human clinical data and outline how tumor copper phenotype, ncRNA signatures, viral etiology, immune context, and individual copper metabolism status could inform precision hepatology. We identify six priority questions and propose a research roadmap to advance this field from correlative associations toward rigorous mechanistic understanding, quantification of cuproptosis relative to established liver-cell death pathways, and eventual clinical implementation in precision hepatology.

title: 2-Hydroxyisobutyrylation of SRSF9 Regulates CD44 Alternative Splicing to Promote Colorectal Cancer Liver Metastasis.
abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) remains a major cause of cancer mortality, yet the metabolic mechanisms that remodel metastatic RNA-splicing programs are poorly defined. Here, integrated quantitative proteomics and lysine 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation (Khib) proteomics of patient-matched normal mucosa, primary CRCs, and liver metastases revealed a progressive increase in global Khib, with enrichment on RNA-splicing proteins. Serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 9 (SRSF9) emerged as a Khib-modified splicing factor whose expression and K155 Khib levels increased from normal tissue to primary tumors and liver metastases. Gain and loss of function studies in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, subcutaneous xenografts, and splenic injection liver metastasis models showed that SRSF9 promotes proliferation, invasion, tumor growth, and liver colonization. Mechanistically, K155 Khib stabilized SRSF9 protein; the K155R mutation accelerated degradation and abolished SRSF9-driven malignant phenotypes. KAT7 and SIRT6 act as regulators of Khib modification, which positively and negatively modulate the K155 Khib modification of SRSF9, respectively. SRSF9 bound CD44 pre-mRNA through its RRM1 domain and promoted alternative splicing toward the oncogenic CD44V8-10 isoform, which was elevated in patient tumors and metastases and rescued the impaired proliferation and metastatic capacity caused by SRSF9 loss. Finally, a CD44V8-10-targeting antisense oligonucleotide suppressed CRC growth and liver metastasis in preclinical models. These findings define a KAT7/SIRT6-regulated Khib-SRSF9-CD44V8-10 axis that couples metabolic acylation to metastatic splicing and nominate CD44V8-10 as a therapeutic vulnerability in CRC liver metastasis.

title: A logic-gated DNA nanocascade for dual-RNA imaging in a triple-negative breast cancer cell model.
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is highly heterogeneous, and accurate molecular subtyping remains challenging because single biomarkers often lack sufficient specificity. Here, we developed an AND logic-gated DNA nanocascade for dual-RNA imaging of miR-21 and PD-L1 mRNA in TNBC cells. The system integrates a miR-21-activated DNAzyme, a PD-L1 mRNA-responsive entropy-driven strand displacement reaction (EDR), and hybridization chain reaction (HCR) amplification. The DNA circuit was encapsulated in Mn-Fe Prussian blue analogue (PBA) metal-organic frameworks and coated with homologous cancer cell membranes to form PBA@DNAzyme-EDR-HCR(DEH)@MDA-MB-231 cell membrane (MM) nanoprobes. The system exhibited detection limits of 0.7 pM for miR-21 and 0.5 pM for PD-L1 mRNA under excess complementary-input conditions and remained responsive when both targets were simultaneously present at 0.5 pM. In MDA-MB-231 cells, simultaneous recognition of both RNA inputs produced strong fluorescence, whereas inhibition of either target markedly reduced the signal. Additional experiments in HCC1806 and AU565 cells further supported differential fluorescence responses across the tested breast cancer cell models. These results demonstrate an AND logic-gated strategy that operates without exogenous protein enzymes and combines dual-RNA recognition with cascade amplification for molecular subtype discrimination.

title: Integrated multi-omics reveals genistein-mediated protection of broiler intestine against heat stress via metabolic-microbial-barrier crosstalk.
abstract: Heat stress severely impairs intestinal health in broilers, highlighting the urgent need for effective nutritional interventions. This study examined whether dietary genistein (150 mg/kg) mitigates heat stress-induced intestinal injury in Ningdu Yellow chickens. A total of 288 one-day-old chicks were assigned to a 2 × 2 arrangement of thermal environment (thermoneutral or intermittent heat stress at 37 ± 2°C) and diet (basal diet or basal diet plus 150 mg/kg genistein), forming four groups: control, genistein, heat stress, and heat stress plus genistein. Duodenal morphology, antioxidant indices, and tight-junction and inflammatory proteins were measured; duodenal transcriptomes, cecal microbiota, and serum metabolites were profiled and integrated by correlation analysis. Phenotypic analyses demonstrated that genistein supplementation significantly (P < 0.05) alleviated heat stress-induced duodenal morphological damage, oxidative stress, barrier injury, and inflammatory responses. RNA sequencing showed that heat stress downregulated duodenal genes in protein processing, metabolic pathways, and tight junction signaling, while genistein reversed suppression of the tight junction pathway, modulated co-expression modules linked to barrier genes, and restored protein levels of CLDN1, CLDN3, CLDN5, and CDC42. Cecal 16S rRNA sequencing showed that genistein partially restored the abundance of beneficial genera (Akkermansia and Lactobacillus) and β-diversity disrupted by heat stress. Serum metabolomic analysis indicated that genistein regulated amino acid metabolism, fatty acid biosynthesis and AMP-activated protein kinase signaling pathways. Multi-omics integration constructed a "metabolic-microbial-intestinal barrier" crosstalk axis, with key correlations including a putative Arg-Trp-Arg feature correlated with Lactobacillus and CLDN3, CLDN11, and JAM3. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that genistein exerts multi-target protective effects against heat stress together with improved duodenal antioxidant and inflammatory indices and changes in microbial-metabolic correlations, thereby providing a theoretical basis for its application as a functional feed additive to mitigate heat stress in poultry.

title: Stage-specific transcriptional atlas of goose satellite cells uncovers sex-biased molecular dynamics associated with embryonic skeletal muscle development.
abstract: Sexual dimorphism in avian skeletal muscle is established during embryogenesis, but the stage-resolved transcriptional programs governing this process in geese remain largely unexplored. To construct a stage-specific transcriptional atlas of muscle satellite cells (SMSCs), we performed histological examination and RNA sequencing of PAX7+ SMSCs isolated from male and female Zhedong White goose embryos across four developmental stages (E13, E15, E18, and E23). Quantitative PCR was used to validate selected differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Although myofiber morphology exhibited no overt sexual divergence, immunofluorescence revealed distinct sex- and stage-dependent dynamics, with male embryos displaying a higher PAX7+ cell abundance at E18 and females at E23. Transcriptomic profiling identified 357, 261, 312, and 672 DEGs at E13, E15, E18, and E23, respectively, uncovering a progressively intensifying sexual bias. At E13, female-biased DEGs were enriched for positional identity genes (HOXC9/C11, HOXD12/13) and pro-proliferative factors (GDF7, FGF16), whereas male-biased DEGs included adhesion molecules (IGSF10/11). At E15, females upregulated genes linked to myofiber maturation (ACTA1, MYH7B) and lipid metabolism (PLIN1, ADIPOQ), while males showed enrichment in extracellular matrix remodeling (MMP7, COL17A1) and immune-related pathways. At E18, females enhanced neuroendocrine signaling (ADCYAP1, AGTR2), whereas males upregulated contractile apparatus components (RYR1, CASQ1) and testis-associated transcripts (BRDT, DHH). By E23, females exhibited signatures of metabolic and neuromuscular optimization, whereas males showed enrichment in extracellular matrix genes (COL11A2, COL9A1/2) and masculinization-associated factors (YBX2, GGN). Temporal pathway analysis demonstrated a progression from immune/chemokine processes at E13, through cytoskeletal organization at E15 and supramolecular fiber components at E18, to DNA metabolism coupled with chemokine signaling at E23. Protein-protein interaction network analysis pinpointed stage-specific hub genes: EGFR (E13), ACTA1/ADIPOQ (E15), RAC2 (E18), and GNG10 (E23). Quantitative PCR validated eight selected DEGs. Collectively, this transcriptional atlas delineates sex-biased molecular dynamics that operate within the Zhedong White goose SMSC pool in the absence of conspicuous histological differences, and provides a foundational gene resource for prioritizing mechanistic investigations into sexually dimorphic muscle development, focusing specifically on the embryonic leg muscles.

title: Convergent and Distinct Transcriptional Signatures in Suicide, Bipolar Disorder, and Major Depressive Disorder.
abstract: Globally, a person dies by suicide every 40 seconds, underscoring a major global public health concern. In the United States, suicide is the second leading cause of death among individuals aged 10-34 years. Suicide is a complex, multifactorial phenomenon influenced by genetic and epigenetic factors and is strongly associated with mood disorders, particularly major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD). However, the extent to which their molecular signatures converge or diverge across disorders and brain regions remains incompletely understood. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review of suicide, MDD, and BD transcriptomic studies in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible studies used human postmortem brain tissue, reported a complete genome-wide transcriptomic list of differentially expressed genes (DEG), and compared suicide decedents with psychiatric non-suicide individuals diagnosed with the same underlying disorder. Regarding BD, studies comparing affected individuals to unaffected controls were included. Single-cell and peripheral-blood studies were excluded because unavailable for suicide. Curated suicide and BD DEG datasets were integrated with a published bulk transcriptomic dataset of MDD. We identified both shared and disease-specific molecular signatures across suicide, BD, and MDD, and identified DEGs shared across brain regions and those that were region-specific. A total of 276 genes were shared across all three conditions, implicating cellular stress, hypoxia (VEGFA, ADM, NDRG1, DDIT4), immune and inflammatory signaling through TNFα/NF-κB (IL1B, ICAM1, NFE2L2) and IL6-JAK-STAT3 pathways (STAT3, SOCS3, IL1R1m OSMR), complement activation (CIR, SERPiNA1, LGALS3), extracellular matrix remodeling (COL4A1, SERPINH1, PLOD2), and unfolded protein response (BAG3, WFS1, MTHFD2). Suicide-associated DEGs were prominently downregulated, and involved metal-ion homeostasis, stress responses, synaptic regulation, and circadian pathways, whereas BD showed downregulation in synaptic and vesicle-related processes alongside region-specific metabolic dysregulation. MDD exhibited changes in RNA processing, ribosomal function, and protein synthesis. Genetic integration revealed that 133 genes shared between BD and MDD had gene variants associated with the corresponding condition per GWAS. Transcription factor analysis identified 20 regulatory factors with altered activity across all three conditions despite differences in their predicted downstream targets. Overall, these findings suggest that suicide, MDD, and BD share aspects of their molecular and regulatory pathophysiology while exhibiting distinct patterns, including in a region-specific manner.

title: Development of siRNAs targeting interferon beta as a novel therapeutic approach for adult and juvenile dermatomyositis.
abstract: A key feature of the autoimmune conditions adult and juvenile dermatomyositis (DM/JDM) is the correlation of interferon (IFN) beta induction with disease initiation and activity. Our aim was to establish a short interfering RNA (siRNA) approach to knockdown IFNB1 expression as a therapeutic strategy for DM/JDM. A library of 74 siRNAs targeting IFNB1 was designed and screened for IFNB1 knockdown by qRT-PCR. Lead siRNAs were analysed for secreted IFN beta protein reduction and acute cytotoxicity. IFNB1 expression was induced for efficacy screening in vitro, including in immortalised myoblasts, myotubes and dermal fibroblasts, alongside JDM patient-derived myotubes. RNA sequencing was also performed on siRNA treated and untreated dermal fibroblasts and patient myotubes. Initial screening of 27 siRNAs identified two lead siRNAs with significant knockdown of both IFN beta transcript and secreted protein in all cell lines, with one lead siRNA demonstrating a more favourable cytotoxicity profile. RNA sequencing and pathway analysis revealed that both lead siRNAs were able to reduce the induction of disease-associated immune and autoimmune pathways in dermal fibroblasts and JDM myotubes. An additional 47 siRNAs across the IFNB1 locus were screened; however, the previous lead siRNA remained the most active across relevant cell lines. Overall, comprehensive in vitro screening identified a lead siRNA targeting IFNB1 with significant mRNA and protein knockdown activity, low cytotoxicity and the ability to modulate immune-relevant pathways in muscle and skin cells. This is a promising first step towards the development of an siRNA therapy for DM/JDM and other conditions driven by IFN beta over-expression.

title: Integrated toxicogenomic and single-nucleus transcriptomic analyses prioritize SDHB and NDUFAB1 in mitochondrial respiration-associated remodeling during cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury.
abstract: Cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury (Cis-AKI) is a multifactorial nephrotoxic syndrome involving proximal tubular injury, oxidative and inflammatory stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic disturbance, and regulated cell death. However, the molecular targets linking cisplatin-associated toxicogenomic changes to AKI remain incompletely characterized. We integrated network toxicology, transcriptomic analysis, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and in vitro experiments to investigate candidate molecular targets in Cis-AKI. Cisplatin-associated toxicogenomic genes were intersected with AKI-related genes, and the shared candidates were analyzed using functional enrichment, protein-protein interaction networks, CytoHubba, and MCODE. Prioritized genes were further examined in a cisplatin-induced mouse Acute kidney injury transcriptomic dataset, a human AKI kidney single-nucleus dataset, proximal tubular pseudotime analysis, and cisplatin-treated BUMPT proximal tubular cells. NicheNet analysis, knockout phenotype annotation, miRNA prediction, candidate compound screening, and molecular docking were also performed. A total of 214 shared genes were identified between the cisplatin-associated and AKI-related gene sets. These genes were mainly enriched in cellular respiration, electron transport, oxidoreductase activity, respiratory-chain complexes, and oxidative phosphorylation. Network analysis prioritized SDHB and NDUFAB1 within the respiration-associated gene network. In the cisplatin-induced mouse AKI dataset, Aco2, Aco1, Sdhb, and Aldh2 were significantly upregulated under stringent criteria, whereas additional respiration- and metabolism-related genes, including Ndufab1, met a secondary differential expression threshold. Human single-nucleus analysis revealed distinct cell-type-specific expression patterns of SDHB and NDUFAB1, with increased SDHB and decreased NDUFAB1 expression in proximal tubular cells. Pseudotime analysis showed a more pronounced late-stage increase in SDHB, whereas NDUFAB1 displayed weaker dynamics. In cisplatin-treated BUMPT cells, Havcr1 and Lcn2 were increased, Bcl2 was decreased, and Casp3 was increased. Among the selected candidate genes, Sdhb, Aco2, Aldh2, Ndufs2, and Uqcrc1 were upregulated, whereas Ndufab1 showed a modest decrease. NicheNet analysis further suggested that TGFB1-related signaling may contribute to proximal tubular transcriptional remodeling. This study prioritizes SDHB and NDUFAB1 within a respiration-associated gene network in Cis-AKI and demonstrates that they exhibit distinct expression patterns during proximal tubular injury. These findings highlight respiration-associated remodeling and proximal tubular state transition in cisplatin-induced kidney injury.

title: A microglial basis for fragile X syndrome via impairment of FMRP-regulated lysosomal function.
abstract: Silencing of the FMRP-encoding FMR1 gene results in fragile X syndrome (FXS), the most common inheritable intellectual disability and autism. FMRP regulates various neuronal functions but clinical trials targeting neurons have failed, suggesting unrecognized disease mechanisms. We find that mice with selective Fmr1 deletion in microglia exhibit audiogenic seizures (AGS) and parvalbumin (PV) neuron loss, recapitulating two key phenotypes observed in FXS (Fmr1-/y) mice. By combining snRNA-Seq and RNA immunoprecipitation, we identify several lysosomal mRNAs as FMRP binding targets. FMRP promotes lysosomal protein expression and its deficiency disrupts lysosomal function in microglia. Notably, FMRP depletion reduces Grn-encoded secretory progranulin and increases PV neuron apoptosis in immature brains. PV neuron density is decreased similarly in Grn+/-, Fmr1-/y, and Grn+/-;Fmr1-/y mice, and progranulin overexpression rescues AGS and PV neuron loss in Fmr1-/y mice. Thus, our study identifies microglia and progranulin as critical regulators of FXS pathogenesis and potential targets for FXS therapy.

title: Genistein targets Wnt5a to alleviate temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis by suppressing JNK/JUN-dependent MMP9 activation.
abstract: Temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis (TMJ-OA) is a progressive degenerative joint disease characterized by cartilage destruction, extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation, and chronic inflammation, yet effective disease-modifying therapeutic targets and pharmacological interventions remain limited. Using a monosodium iodoacetate (MIA)-induced rat TMJ-OA model and interleukin-1β (IL-1β)-stimulated chondrocytes, we integrated transcriptomic analysis, chromatin accessibility profiling, and molecular screening to elucidate disease mechanisms and identify candidate compounds. Integrated RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis revealed Wnt family member 5a (Wnt5a) as a critical upstream regulator significantly associated with TMJ-OA progression, while assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) uncovered an inflammatory chromatin landscape characterized by enhanced activator protein-1 (AP-1) activity and JUN-dependent transcriptional regulation ofmatrix metalloproteinase 9 (Mmp9). Mechanistically, Wnt5a activated c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling to promote JUN nuclear accumulation and enhance AP-1-mediatedMmp9transcription, leading to ECM degradation and chondrocyte dysfunction. Structure-based virtual screening and biophysical assays, including surface plasmon resonance (SPR), cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), and drug affinity responsive target stability (DARTS), identified genistein (GEN) as a small-molecule compound capable of directly binding Wnt5a, supported by cellular target-engagement evidence. Functionally, genistein suppressed the Wnt5a/JNK/JUN/MMP9 signaling axis, partially restored type II collagen (COL2A1) expression, alleviated oxidative stress, and preserved cartilage integrity in TMJ-OA rats. Collectively, these findings establish Wnt5a as a therapeutically actionable driver of TMJ-OA progression and identify genistein as a Wnt5a-targeting compound with cartilage-protective activity, providing a mechanism-based rationale for developing disease-modifying interventions for degenerative joint diseases.

title: The future of brain tumor treatment: integrating platelet-based liquid biopsy, advanced drug delivery systems, and eicosanoid inhibition.
abstract: Despite extensive research, brain tumors still have some of the lowest survival rates among cancers. Their marked resistance to both conventional and emerging therapies stems from the unique properties of neural cells and their microenvironment, including the blood-brain barrier, cellular heterogeneity, and an immunosuppressive milieu. Addressing these challenges is essential for developing effective therapeutic strategies that improve patient outcomes. Advancements in brain tumor treatment depend on understanding the biological mechanisms behind potential drug targets and developing appropriate drug discovery strategies to inhibit them effectively. A major barrier remains the difficulty many drugs face in crossing the blood-brain barrier, which greatly restrains treatment effectiveness in brain tumor patients. Therefore, developing innovative drug delivery systems is essential. The brain exhibits a high concentration of fatty acids, notably polyunsaturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid (AA), which are primarily esterified within membrane phospholipids. Upon release, cyclooxygenases, lipoxygenases, and cytochrome P450 enzymes can transform AA into various eicosanoid classes, producing lipid mediators involved in signal transduction pathways that regulate neurotransmission, neuroinflammation, and neuroplasticity.
